title: 大智度論
text: 佛告須菩提：「三千大千世界中諸惡魔皆愁毒，如箭入心，各於其坐不能自安。須菩提！菩薩摩訶薩能如是行般若波羅蜜，是時一切世間天及人、阿修羅不能得其便令其憂惱。須菩提！以是故，菩薩摩訶薩欲得阿耨多羅三藐三菩提，當行是般若波羅蜜！菩薩摩訶薩行般若波羅蜜時，具足修檀波羅蜜、尸羅波羅蜜、羼提波羅蜜、毘梨耶波羅蜜、禪波羅蜜、般若波羅蜜。須菩提！菩薩摩訶薩行般若波羅蜜時，具足諸波羅蜜。」
without: The Buddha said to Subhūti, "In the three-thousand-fold great thousand-fold world, all the evil demons are sorrowful and pained, as if an arrow had entered their hearts, and each is unable to remain at ease in his seat. Subhūti, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva can practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) in this way, at that time all the gods, humans, and antigods (asura) of the world cannot find an opportunity to cause him worry or affliction. Subhūti, for this reason, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who wishes to attain supreme perfect enlightenment (anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi) should practice this perfection of wisdom. When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he fully cultivates the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā), the perfection of morality (śīlapāramitā), the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā), the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā), the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā), and the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he fulfills all the perfections (pāramitā)."
with: The Blessed One said to Subhūti: "In the three-thousand-great-thousand world-system, all the māras are sorrowful and pained, as if an arrow had entered their hearts, and each is unable to remain at ease in his seat. Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā in this way, at that time all the gods, humans, and asuras of the world cannot find an opportunity to cause him worry or affliction. Subhūti, for this reason, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to attain anuttara samyaksambodhi should practice this prajñāpāramitā. When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, he fulfills the dānapāramitā, the śīlapāramitā, the kṣāntipāramitā, the vīryapāramitā, the dhyānapāramitā, and the prajñāpāramitā. Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, he fulfills all the pāramitās."

title: 大智度論
text: 佛告須菩提：「色如相，受、想、行、識如相，乃至涅槃如相，是阿耨多羅三藐三菩提。是如相亦不增不減。須菩提！是菩薩摩訶薩不離般若波羅蜜，常觀是如法，不見有增有減。以是因緣故，須菩提！不可說義無增無減，檀波羅蜜亦不增不減，乃至十八不共法亦不增不減。須菩提！菩薩摩訶薩以是不增不減法故，應般若波羅蜜行。」
without: The Buddha said to Subhūti: "The nature of form (rūpa) is the nature of suchness (tathatā), and the nature of feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), volitional formations (saṃskāra), and consciousness (vijñāna) is the nature of suchness, up to and including the nature of suchness of nirvana; this is supreme, perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi). This nature of suchness neither increases nor decreases. Subhūti, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not depart from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), constantly contemplating this dharma of suchness, seeing neither increase nor decrease. For this reason, Subhūti, the ineffable meaning is without increase or decrease; the perfection of generosity (dāna-pāramitā) also neither increases nor decreases, up to and including the eighteen exclusive qualities of a Buddha (āveṇika-dharma) which also neither increase nor decrease. Subhūti, because of this dharma of neither increase nor decrease, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)."
with: The Buddha said to Subhūti: "The nature of form is the nature of suchness (tathatā), and the nature of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness is the nature of suchness, up to and including the nature of suchness of nirvāṇa; this is the unexcelled, perfect awakening (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi). This nature of suchness neither increases nor decreases. Subhūti, this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not depart from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā); he constantly contemplates this dharma of suchness and does not perceive any increase or decrease. For this reason, Subhūti, the inexpressible (anabhilāpya) meaning has no increase or decrease; the perfection of generosity (dāna-pāramitā) also neither increases nor decreases, up to and including the eighteen exclusive qualities of a Buddha (aṣṭādaśāveṇikabuddhadharma) which also neither increase nor decrease. Subhūti, because of this dharma of non-increase and non-decrease, the bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)."

title: 大智度論
text: 佛言：「不與不善法合，不與善法合；不與世間法合，不與出世間法合；不與有漏法合，不與無漏法合；不與有罪法合，不與無罪法合；不與有為法合，不與無為法合。何以故？般若波羅蜜不為得諸法故生，以是故於諸法無所合。」
without: The Buddha said: "It does not combine with unwholesome states, nor does it combine with wholesome states; it does not combine with worldly states, nor does it combine with supramundane states; it does not combine with states involving outflows (āsrava), nor does it combine with states free from outflows; it does not combine with states that are faulty, nor does it combine with states that are faultless; it does not combine with conditioned states (saṃskṛta), nor does it combine with unconditioned states (asaṃskṛta). Why is this? The perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) does not arise for the sake of attaining any states; for this reason, it does not combine with any states."
with: The Buddha said: "It does not combine with unwholesome dharmas, nor does it combine with wholesome dharmas; it does not combine with worldly (laukika) dharmas, nor does it combine with supramundane dharmas; it does not combine with tainted (āsrava) dharmas, nor does it combine with untainted (anāsrava-dharma) dharmas; it does not combine with faulty dharmas, nor does it combine with faultless (anavadya) dharmas; it does not combine with conditioned (saṃskṛta) dharmas, nor does it combine with unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) dharmas. What is the reason for this? The perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) does not arise for the sake of attaining any dharmas; for this reason, it does not combine with any dharmas."

title: 大智度論
text: 佛告須菩提：「信般若波羅蜜，則不信色，不信受、想、行、識；不信眼乃至意；不信色乃至法；不信眼界乃至意識界；不信檀波羅蜜、尸羅波羅蜜、羼提波羅蜜、毘梨耶波羅蜜、禪波羅蜜；不信內空乃至無法有法空；不信四念處乃至八聖道分；不信佛十力乃至十八不共法；不信須陀洹果、斯陀含果、阿那含果、阿羅漢果、辟支佛道；不信菩薩道；不信阿耨多羅三藐三菩提乃至一切種智。」
without: The Buddha said to Subhūti: "To have faith in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is to have no faith in form, no faith in feeling, perception, volitional formations, or consciousness; no faith in the eye up to the mind; no faith in visible objects up to mental objects; no faith in the eye-element up to the mind-consciousness element; no faith in the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā), the perfection of moral discipline (śīlapāramitā), the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā), the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā), or the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā); no faith in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence and existence of things; no faith in the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; no faith in the ten powers of a buddha up to the eighteen special attributes; no faith in the fruit of a stream-enterer, the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, the fruit of an arhat, or the path of a solitary buddha; no faith in the bodhisattva path; and no faith in unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment (anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi) up to omniscience."
with: The Buddha said to Subhūti: “To believe in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is to not believe in form, and to not believe in feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness; it is to not believe in the eye up to the mind; it is to not believe in visible objects up to mental objects; it is to not believe in the eye-element up to the mind-consciousness element; it is to not believe in the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā), the perfection of moral discipline (śīlapāramitā), the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā), the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā), and the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā); it is to not believe in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existent and existent things; it is to not believe in the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path (ārya-mārga); it is to not believe in the ten powers of a buddha (daśabala) up to the eighteen special attributes of a buddha; it is to not believe in the fruit of a stream-enterer, the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, the fruit of an arhat (arhant-phala), or the path of a solitary buddha; it is to not believe in the bodhisattva path; it is to not believe in unsurpassed, perfect awakening (samyaksambodhi) up to the omniscience of all aspects (sarva-ākārajña).”

title: 瑜伽師地論
text: 復次，無想等至，當言唯一有漏。滅盡等至當言無漏。由與煩惱不相應故、非相應故、無所緣故、非諸煩惱之所生故。是出世間，一切異生不能行故。唯除已入遠地菩薩。菩薩雖能起出世法，令現在前，然由方便善巧力故，不捨煩惱。又此等至，當言非學非無學攝，非所行故，似涅槃故。
without: Furthermore, the attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñā-samāpatti) should be spoken of as exclusively tainted (sāsrava). The attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) should be spoken of as untainted (anāsrava), because it is not associated with afflictions (kleśa), because it is not connected with them, because it has no object of perception (ālambana), and because it is not produced by any afflictions. It is supramundane (lokottara), because all ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) are unable to enter it, with the sole exception of bodhisattvas who have entered the distant stages (dūraṃgamā-bhūmi). Although a bodhisattva is able to manifest supramundane states, through the power of skillful means (upāya-kauśalya) they do not abandon the afflictions. Moreover, this attainment should be spoken of as being included neither in the state of a learner (śaikṣa) nor in the state of a non-learner (aśaikṣa), because it is not an object of practice and because it resembles nirvana.
with: Furthermore, the attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñin) should be spoken of as exclusively tainted (āsrava). The attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) should be spoken of as untainted (anāsrava), because it is not associated with the afflictions (kleśa), because it is not conjoined with them, because it has no object of perception, and because it is not produced by any of the afflictions (kleśa). It is supramundane (lokottara), because all ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) are unable to practice it, with the sole exception of those bodhisattvas who have entered the distant stages. Although a bodhisattva is able to manifest supramundane phenomena (lokottara-dharma), through the power of skillful means (upāya-kauśalya) they do not abandon the afflictions (kleśa). Moreover, this attainment should be spoken of as being included neither in the category of the learner nor in the category of the non-learner, because it is not a field of activity (gocara) and because it resembles nirvana (nirvāṇa).

title: 瑜伽師地論
text: 云何菩薩善士精進？謂此精進略有五種。一、無所棄捨精進。謂諸菩薩所有精進，不捨一切欲加行故。二、無退減精進。謂諸菩薩所有精進，如先所受若等若增，發勤精進隨長養故。三、無下劣精進。謂諸菩薩所有精進，勇猛、熾然、長時、無間精勤策勵，心無怯弱、無退屈故。四、無顛倒精進。謂諸菩薩所有精進，能引義利，方便善巧所攝持故。五、勤勇加行精進。謂諸菩薩所有精進，能於無上正等菩提達進趣故。
without:
What is the exertion (vīrya) of a bodhisattva of good character? In brief, this exertion has five kinds.

First, the exertion of not abandoning. This means that the exertion possessed by bodhisattvas does not abandon any of the applications of desire.

Second, the exertion of not diminishing. This means that the exertion possessed by bodhisattvas is such that, whether equal to or greater than what was previously undertaken, they arouse and cultivate exertion accordingly.

Third, the exertion of not being inferior. This means that the exertion possessed by bodhisattvas is brave, ardent, long-lasting, and unceasing in its diligent application, with a mind that is neither timid nor discouraged.

Fourth, the exertion of not being inverted. This means that the exertion possessed by bodhisattvas is able to lead to benefit and is supported by skillful means (upāya).

Fifth, the exertion of diligent application. This means that the exertion possessed by bodhisattvas is able to advance toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
with:
What is the exertion (vīrya) of a bodhisattva of good character? This exertion is briefly of five kinds.

First, the exertion of non-abandonment. This means that the exertion of all bodhisattvas does not abandon any of the desired applications (prayoga).

Second, the exertion of non-diminishment. This means that the exertion of all bodhisattvas, whether equal to or greater than what was previously undertaken, is cultivated and nurtured through diligent effort.

Third, the exertion of non-inferiority (avara). This means that the exertion of all bodhisattvas is courageous, intense, long-term (dīrgha-kāla), and uninterrupted (anantarya), with a mind that is neither timid nor discouraged.

Fourth, the exertion of non-perversion. This means that the exertion of all bodhisattvas is able to lead to benefit (artha) and is sustained by skillful means (upāya-kauśalya).

Fifth, the exertion of diligent application (prayoga). This means that the exertion of all bodhisattvas is able to advance toward the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening (anuttara samyaksambodhi).

title: 瑜伽師地論
text: 善男子！我亦依法無我性所顯勝義無自性性，密意說言一切諸法無生無滅、本來寂靜、自性涅槃。何以故？法無我性所顯勝義無自性性，於常常時、於恒恒時，諸法法性安住無為，一切雜染不相應故；於常常時、於恒恒時，諸法法性安住故無為。由無為故，無生無滅；一切雜染不相應故，本來寂靜、自性涅槃。是故我依法無我性所顯勝義無自性性，密意說言一切諸法無生無滅、本來寂靜、自性涅槃。
without: "Good son, based on the ultimate nature of non-essence (niḥsvabhāvatā) revealed by the nature of the non-self of phenomena (dharmanairātmya), I have spoken with hidden intent that all phenomena are without birth, without cessation, originally quiescent, and by nature in nirvana. Why is this? Because the ultimate nature of non-essence revealed by the nature of the non-self of phenomena is, at all times and at all moments, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) abiding as unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), being disconnected from all defilements. Because it is unconditioned, it is without birth and without cessation; because it is disconnected from all defilements, it is originally quiescent and by nature in nirvana. Therefore, based on the ultimate nature of non-essence revealed by the nature of the non-self of phenomena, I have spoken with hidden intent that all phenomena are without birth, without cessation, originally quiescent, and by nature in nirvana."
with: "Good son, based on the ultimate nature of non-essence (svabhāva) manifested by the nature of the non-self of phenomena (dharma), I have spoken with hidden intent, saying: 'All phenomena (dharma) are without arising, without cessation, originally quiescent, and by nature in nirvana.' Why is this? Because the ultimate nature of non-essence manifested by the nature of the non-self of phenomena is, at all times and at all moments, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) abiding as the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), being disconnected from all defilement (saṃkleśa). Because it abides as the nature of phenomena at all times and at all moments, it is the unconditioned. Because it is the unconditioned, it is without arising and without cessation; and because it is disconnected from all defilement, it is originally quiescent and by nature in nirvana. Therefore, based on the ultimate nature of non-essence manifested by the nature of the non-self of phenomena, I have spoken with hidden intent, saying: 'All phenomena are without arising, without cessation, originally quiescent, and by nature in nirvana.'"

title: 瑜伽師地論
text: 答：當正了知唯有其名、唯遍計執，無相、無性、無生、無滅、無染、無淨，本來寂靜、自性涅槃，非過去、非未來、非現在，非繫、非離繫，非縛、非解脫，非苦、非樂、非不苦不樂，唯是一味，遍一切處皆如虛空。以如是等無量行相，應正了知遍計所執自性。
without: Response: One should correctly understand that it is only a name, only an imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva), without characteristics, without intrinsic nature, without arising, without ceasing, without defilement, without purification; it is originally tranquil, by nature nirvana, not of the past, not of the future, not of the present, neither bound nor unbound, neither fettered nor liberated, neither suffering, nor pleasant, nor neither-suffering-nor-pleasant; it is only of one flavor, and everywhere it is like space. By means of these and other immeasurable aspects, one should correctly understand the imagined nature.
with: Response: One should correctly understand that there is only a name, only an imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva), without characteristics (animitta), without intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva), without arising (anutpāda), without ceasing, without defilement, without purification, originally tranquil, by nature liberated (svabhāva-nirvāṇa), not of the past, not of the future, not of the present, neither bound nor unbound, neither fettered nor liberated, neither suffering nor pleasant nor neither-suffering-nor-pleasant, being only of one flavor, and everywhere like space (ākāśa). By such immeasurable aspects (ākāra), one should correctly understand the imagined nature.

title: 雜阿含經
text: 佛告阿濕波誓：「若沙門、婆羅門三昧堅固，三昧平等，若不得入彼三昧，不應作念：『我於三昧退減。』若復聖弟子不見色是我、異我、相在，不見受、想、行、識是我、異我、相在，但當作是覺知：『貪欲永盡無餘，瞋恚、愚癡永盡無餘。』貪、恚、癡永盡無餘已，一切漏盡，無漏心解脫、慧解脫，現法自知作證：『我生已盡，梵行已立，所作已作，自知不受後有。』」
without: The Buddha said to Aggivessana: "If a renunciant or a brahmin has firm concentration and balanced concentration, yet cannot enter that concentration, he should not think: 'I have regressed from concentration.' If a noble disciple does not see bodily form as self, as different from self, or as existing within self, and does not see feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness as self, as different from self, or as existing within self, he should simply be aware: 'Greed is eradicated without remainder, hatred is eradicated without remainder, and delusion is eradicated without remainder.' Once greed, hatred, and delusion are eradicated without remainder, all influxes (āsrava) are destroyed, and he attains influx-free liberation of the mind and liberation by wisdom, personally knowing and realizing here and now: 'Birth for me has been eradicated, the holy life has been established, what had to be done has been done, I myself know that there will be no receiving of further existence.'"
with: The Buddha said to Aśvajit: “If a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa has a samādhi that is firm and a samādhi that is balanced, and if he does not attain entry into that samādhi, he should not think: ‘I have regressed in samādhi.’ If, furthermore, a noble disciple does not see bodily form as self, as different from self, or as existing within self, and does not see feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness as self, as different from self, or as existing within self, he should simply be aware of this: ‘Greed (kāma-rāga) is forever ended without remainder; hatred and delusion are forever ended without remainder.’ When greed, hatred, and delusion are forever ended without remainder, all influxes are ended, and he attains the influx-free liberation of the mind and liberation by wisdom. Here and now (dṛṣṭadharma), he personally knows and realizes: ‘Birth for me has been eradicated, the holy life (brahmacarya) has been established, what had to be done (kṛtya) has been done, and I myself know that there will be no receiving of further existence (punarbhava).’”

title: 雜阿含經
text: 「若諸善法生，一切皆明為根本，明集、明生、明起。明，於善、不善法如實知者，罪、無罪，親近、不親近，卑法、勝法，穢污、白淨，有分別、無分別，緣起、非緣起悉如實知，如實知者，是則正見。正見者，能起正志、正語、正業、正命、正方便、正念、正定。正定起已，聖弟子得正解脫貪、恚、癡，貪、恚、癡解脫已，是聖弟子得正智見：『我生已盡，梵行已立，所作已作，自知不受後有。』」
without: "Whatever wholesome states arise, all have clarity (vidyā) as their root, clarity as their gathering, clarity as their origin, and clarity as their arising. Clarity is the knowing of wholesome and unwholesome states as they truly are: knowing what is blameworthy and blameless, what should be cultivated and what should not be cultivated, what is inferior and what is superior, what is stained and what is pure, what is with discrimination and what is without discrimination, and what is dependent on conditions and what is not dependent on conditions—all this one knows as it truly is. Knowing as it truly is, this is right view. From right view, one is able to give rise to right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. Once right concentration has arisen, the noble disciple attains right liberation from greed, hatred, and delusion. Once liberated from greed, hatred, and delusion, this noble disciple attains right knowledge and vision, knowing: 'Birth for me has been eradicated, the holy life has been established, what had to be done has been done, I myself know that there will be no receiving of any further existence.'"
with: “If any wholesome states arise, all of them have clarity (vidyā) as their root, clarity as their gathering, clarity as their arising, and clarity as their inception. Clarity is the knowing of wholesome and unwholesome states as they truly are: knowing what is blameworthy and blameless, what should be cultivated and what should not be cultivated, what is inferior and what is superior, what is defiled and what is pure, what is with discrimination (vikalpa) and what is without discrimination (nirvikalpa), and what is dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) and what is not dependent origination—all of these one knows as they truly are. One who knows as they truly are possesses right view (samyagdṛṣṭi). Possessing right view, one is able to give rise to right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort (upāya), right mindfulness (smṛti), and right concentration. Once right concentration has arisen, the noble disciple attains right liberation (vimukti) from greed, hatred, and delusion. Once liberated from greed, hatred, and delusion, this noble disciple attains right knowledge and vision: ‘Birth for me has been eradicated, the holy life (brahmacarya) has been established, what had to be done (kṛtya) has been done, I myself know that there will be no receiving of any further existence.’”

title: 雜阿含經
text: 爾時，世尊告諸比丘：「轉輪王七寶具足，成就人中四種神力，王四天下，身壞命終，生於天上。雖復轉輪聖王七寶具足，成就人間神力，王四天下，身壞命終，得生天上，然猶未斷地獄、畜生、餓鬼惡趣之苦。所以者何？以轉輪王不得於佛不壞淨，法、僧不壞淨，聖戒不成就故。
without: At that time, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "A wheel-turning king (cakravartin) is endowed with the seven treasures and possesses the four kinds of human power. He rules over the four continents, and upon the breaking up of the body after death, he is reborn in the heavenly realms. Although a noble wheel-turning king is endowed with the seven treasures, possesses human power, rules over the four continents, and upon the breaking up of the body after death is reborn in the heavenly realms, he has still not cut off the suffering of the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts. Why is this? Because the wheel-turning king has not attained the unwavering confidence (prasāda) in the Buddha, the unwavering confidence in the Dharma, the unwavering confidence in the Sangha, and has not perfected the noble moral discipline (śīla)."
with: At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus: "The cakravartin possesses the seven jewels (saptaratna), attains the four kinds of divine power among humans, and rules over the four continents; yet, upon the breaking up of the body after death, he is reborn in the heavenly realm. Although the noble cakravartin possesses the seven jewels, attains divine power among humans, and rules over the four continents, upon the breaking up of the body after death he is reborn in the heavenly realm, yet he has not cut off the suffering of the naraka, the tiryañc, and the preta, the states of woe (apāya). What is the reason for this? It is because the cakravartin has not attained the unwavering purity of the Buddha, the unwavering purity of the Dharma and the Saṅgha, and has not attained the noble śīla."

title: 雜阿含經
text: 時，婆羅門即作是念：「過去世中有無量恒河沙等諸佛世尊，我曾不習近。設復未來如無量恒河沙三藐三佛陀，亦當不與習近娛樂。我今當於沙門瞿曇所修行梵行。」即便合掌白佛言：「唯願聽我於正法、律出家修梵行。」
without: At that time, the brahmin thought to himself: "In the past, there were Buddhas, Blessed Ones, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, whom I did not attend. And in the future, there will be perfectly and fully awakened Buddhas (samyaksambuddha) as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, whom I will also not attend or take delight in. I shall now cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya) under the recluse Gotama." He then joined his palms together and said to the Buddha: "I wish to be permitted to go forth from home into homelessness in this right teaching and discipline (dharma-vinaya) to cultivate the holy life."
with: At that time, the brāhmaṇa (brāhmaṇa) thought to himself: "In the past there were Buddha-bhagavants (buddha bhagavant) as numerous as the sands of the Ganges (gaṅgā-nadī-vālukā), yet I never drew near to them. Even if in the future there are samyaksambuddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, I will likewise not draw near to them or find delight in them. I shall now cultivate the holy life under the śramaṇa gautama (śramaṇa gautama)." He then joined his palms together and said to the Buddha: "I only wish that you would allow me to go forth (pravrajyā) in this saddharma (saddharma) and discipline to cultivate the holy life."

title: 阿毘達磨俱舍論
text: 論曰：由田勝者，聞有苾芻於僧眾中作女人語，彼於現世轉作女人。此等傳聞其類非一。由意勝者，聞有黃門救脫諸牛黃門事故，彼於現世轉作丈夫。此等傳聞事亦非一。或生此地永離此地染，於此地中諸善不善業。於異熟定位不定者，此業必能招現法果。若有餘位順定受業，彼必定無永離染義，必於餘位受異熟果。若於異熟亦不定者，永離染故不受異熟。何田起業定即受耶？頌曰：
without:
The treatise says: Regarding the excellence of the field, it is heard that there was a monk (bhikṣu) who spoke like a woman in the midst of the monastic community, and because of that, he was transformed into a woman in this very lifetime. Such reports are not singular. Regarding the excellence of intention, it is heard that there was a eunuch (paṇḍaka) who saved cows from the business of being eunuchs, and because of that, he was transformed into a man in this very lifetime. Such reports are also not singular.

As for wholesome or unwholesome actions performed in this place by one who is born in this place and has permanently abandoned the defilements (kleśa) of this place: if the ripening (vipāka) is certain but the timing is uncertain, this action will inevitably bring about a result in the present lifetime. If there is an action that is certain to be experienced in another lifetime, it is certain that there is no meaning in having permanently abandoned the defilements, and one will necessarily experience the ripening in another lifetime. If the ripening itself is also uncertain, then because the defilements have been permanently abandoned, one does not experience the ripening.

From what field does an action arise such that it is certain to be experienced? The verse says:
with:
The treatise says: Regarding the superiority of the field, it is heard that there was a bhikṣu who spoke as a woman among the saṃgha, and he was transformed into a woman in this very lifetime. Such reports are not singular. Regarding the superiority of intention, it is heard that there was a eunuch who saved cattle from a eunuch’s affair, and he was transformed into a puruṣa in this very lifetime. Such reports are also not singular.

Regarding actions that are wholesome or unwholesome in this realm, for one who is born in this realm and permanently attains vairāgya in this realm: if the vipāka is certain but the timing is aniyata, this action will inevitably bring about a dṛṣṭadharma result. If the action is one that is certain to be experienced in another lifetime, then because there is no possibility of permanent vairāgya, it will inevitably experience its vipāka in that other lifetime. If the vipāka itself is also aniyata, then because one has attained permanent vairāgya, one will not experience the vipāka.

From what field does an action arise such that it is certain to be experienced? The gāthā says:

title: 成唯識論
text: 云何漸次悟入唯識？謂諸菩薩於識相、性，資糧位中能深信解；在加行位能漸伏除所取、能取，引發真見；在通達位如實通達；修習位中如所見理，數數修習伏斷餘障；至究竟位出障圓明，能盡未來化有情類，復令悟入唯識相、性。
without: How does one gradually awaken to and enter into Consciousness-Only (vijñaptimātra)? It is said that Bodhisattvas, during the stage of provisioning (saṃbhāra-mārga), are able to deeply believe in and understand the characteristics and nature of consciousness. During the stage of applied effort (prayoga-mārga), they are able to gradually subdue and eliminate the grasped and the grasper, thereby inducing true vision. During the stage of realization (darśana-mārga), they realize these things as they truly are. During the stage of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga), they repeatedly practice in accordance with the principles they have perceived to subdue and sever the remaining hindrances. Arriving at the ultimate stage (niṣṭhā-mārga), they emerge from obstacles with perfect clarity, able to transform all classes of sentient beings until the end of time, and cause them to awaken to and enter the characteristics and nature of Consciousness-Only.
with: How does one gradually awaken to and enter Consciousness-Only? It means that Bodhisattvas, during the stage of provisioning (sambhāra), are able to deeply believe in and understand the characteristics and nature of consciousness; during the stage of applied effort (prayoga), they are able to gradually subdue and eliminate the grasped (grāhya) and the grasper (grāhaka) to induce true vision; during the stage of realization (prativedha), they realize them as they truly are (yathābhūtam); during the stage of cultivation (bhāvanā), they repeatedly practice in accordance with the principles they have perceived to subdue and sever the remaining hindrances; and upon arriving at the ultimate stage (niṣṭhā), they emerge from obstacles with perfect clarity, able to transform all classes of sentient beings until the end of time (anāgata), and cause them to awaken to and enter the characteristics and nature of Consciousness-Only.

title: 阿毘達磨俱舍論
text: 論曰：善無漏法亦名為妙。諸染污法亦名有罪有覆及劣。准此妙劣，餘中已成，故頌不辯。諸有為善亦名應習，餘非應習義准已成。何故無為不名應習？不可數習令增長故。又習為果，此無果故。解脫涅槃亦名無上，以無一法能勝涅槃，是善是常超眾法故。餘法有上，義准已成。
without: The treatise says: Virtuous, undefiled phenomena (anāsrava-dharma) are also called excellent. All defiled phenomena are also called faulty, obstructive, and inferior. Based on these categories of excellent and inferior, the status of the remainder is already established by implication, and therefore the verse does not discuss it. All conditioned virtuous phenomena are also called worthy of cultivation; the fact that others are not worthy of cultivation is likewise established by implication. Why is the unconditioned not called worthy of cultivation? Because it cannot be repeatedly cultivated to cause it to increase. Furthermore, cultivation has a result, and this has no result. Liberation and Nirvana are also called supreme, because no phenomenon can surpass Nirvana, as it is virtuous, eternal, and transcends all phenomena. That other phenomena have something superior to them is already established by implication.
with: The treatise says: Wholesome, undefiled phenomena (anāsrava-dharma) are also called excellent. All defiled phenomena are also called faulty, covered, and inferior. Based on these categories of excellent and inferior, the status of the remaining phenomena is already established by implication, and therefore the verse does not discuss them. All conditioned wholesome phenomena are also called worthy of practice; the fact that others are not worthy of practice is established by implication. Why is the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) not called worthy of practice? Because it cannot be practiced repeatedly to cause growth. Furthermore, practice has a result, and this has no result. Liberation (vimokṣa) and Nirvana (nirvāṇa) are also called supreme (anuttara), because no single phenomenon can surpass Nirvana, as it is wholesome, eternal (nitya), and transcends all phenomena. That other phenomena have something superior to them is established by implication.
